newsitem.title: UK: Houston Ship Channel plan to involve some closures.
newsitem.headline: Houston Ship Channel plan to involve some closures.

text.p: The new plan to limit disruption to shipping while a tunnel under the Houston Ship Channel is removed will involve some closures, according to Texas transport authorities.

Texas Department of Transportation director of construction for the Houston area, Dennis Warren said the winning bid for the project allowed for a schedule of closures agreed with Port of Houston users.
"We have worked out a schedule for the duration of channel closures and partial closures with the port users which will have a minimal effect on them," Warren said.
"The contractor has the right to make five 12-hour long full channel closures. But we will pay them a bonus if they do not need to use them," he said.
Warren added, "We have also worked out a schedule so that partial closures can be made every other day during the work to remove the tunnel."

Partial closures would mean reducing the width of parts of the shipping channel to 300 feet from its actual width of around 450 feet, Warren said. The channel is given a theoretical width of 400 feet.
Houston-based Williams Brothers Construction Co has won the contract to remove the Baytown tunnel with a $17.6 million bid. It was in competition with four other firms.
It is expected that work will begin in late August or early September after the contract is officially awarded at the end of July.
A completion date will be set by the contractor when it has been able to undertake further evaluation after beginning work, a spokeswoman for the Port of Houston Authority said.
Houston maritime officials sought new bidders for the work to remove the tunnel after earlier this year rejecting a plan which it was feared could lead to 55 closures of the channel.

The tunnel has to be removed before the Houston Ship Channel's depth is increased by 5 feet to 45 feet and its width extended to 530 feet. Dredging will be carried out by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers next year if funding is approved by the U.S. Congress.
Tanker owners had previously expressed concerns at the possibility of delays to berthing during the tunnel works.
Dredging will allow more fully laden tankers and container ships to navigate the channel which links Houston's port and refinery row to the Gulf of Mexico.
